newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Luck a factor in making Canadian laws.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Luck a factor in making Canadian laws.

text.p: For a Canadian member of Parliament, legislation is a matter of lottery and luck, unless you are a government minister.

Bills introduced by backbenchers, whether they are members of the governing party or the opposition, get thrown into a bin and are drawn at random for the slim chance to pass the House of Commons. If a so-called private member does strike it lucky, a small subcommittee examines his bill to decide whether or not to declare it "votable" -- whether to allow it to have a chance of passing. Two-thirds are declared non-votable.

"(The system) makes private members' bills a sham," said Keith Martin, a legislator from the opposition Reform Party who managed to get a bill calling for a domestic ban on land mines out of the lottery only to have it labeled non-votable. "We're the only so-called democracy in the world that has non-votable private members' bills. It makes a mockery of the democratic process."

Even if private bills pass through the gantlet of the lottery and the subcommittee, the government -- currently Liberal -- tends to use its power to see to it that they are almost certain to be voted down or die in committee.
TWO LAWS OUT OF 152 BILLS
In 1996 private members introduced 152 bills. Only 50 were picked in the lottery and only two made it into law.

In Washington, members of the House or Senate who introduce bills may seek co-sponsors from both parties and can try to push the legislation through -- although they too have to manoeuvre past the political bureaucracy running Congress.
One of the main reasons for the Canadian system is to find some method of managing a legislative programme when the House of Commons meets only about 34 hours a week, 27 weeks a year.

"Frankly, if every idea from every MP were made votable, we'd have a very long, drawn-out process and it would all lose its effectiveness," Carolyn Parrish, chairwoman of the subcommittee that screens private members' bills, said.
Whatever the reason, the system discourages members of Parliament on both sides of the aisle unless they are cabinet ministers.

Liberal member Paul Szabo put his bill, which would require alcohol distributors to put warning labels on their products, in the bin in June 1995. Nearly a year and a half later it is still stuck in the system. The bill was declared votable, was read in the House of Commons and was supported by all parties, but it was sent to the health committee for consideration and is unlikely to be returned to the House for a final vote.
"I can't get it out (of the committee)," Szabo said. "It's as good as dead."
WHERE TO PUT THE BLAME
Szabo was cautious in assigning blame for his troubles in getting the bill passed, but Martin had no such qualms.

"The government does not want to see any substantial private member's bill go through because if anything substantial is going to go through they want to make sure they have their stamp on it, rather than have a private member upstage the government of the day," Martin said. "We live in a fiefdom, not a democracy, and control is centred in the PMO (prime minister's office)..., a few cabinet ministers and a few captains in industry. Everyone else here is superfluous to the situation."
Non-votable bills are debated only for an hour in Parliament and then unceremoniously dropped.

Some parliamentarians point to the subcommittee for private members' business as the government's "gatekeeper," but Parrish said the government does not give her instructions. "I am not a gatekeeper, I've never been approached by any member of the government to tell me to watch out for a controversial bill coming through. My job there is to direct traffic," she said.

But she conceded the system needs an overhaul and said the subcommittee has been studying ways of circumventing the lottery process and making more bills votable. The subcommittee is scheduled to report in March on possible changes to the system.

Martin says the system needs to be changed to resemble more closely that of the United States, where private bills put forward by individual members of Congress have a much better chance of becoming law.
"We need to look at a hybrid model of what goes on here and what goes on in the United States -- one that gives private members more power," he said.
